concept.title: Headings
concept.abstract: This section covers the Heading style in DOCX — its role as the primary structural mechanism that organizes a document's content into a named, hierarchical sequence of sections — and four scenarios: headings applied in correct sequential order, a heading level skipped in the hierarchy, a top-level heading absent from the document, and consecutive headings with no body content between them. The converter reads each heading level to construct the DITA map hierarchy, generating sub-maps, topic files, and topic type classifications from the heading sequence and the content that follows each heading.

conbody.p: A Heading style marks the beginning of a named section of content and assigns it a rank in the document hierarchy. It is the primary structural mechanism of any technical document — headings divide continuous content into discrete, named units, establish the parent-child relationships between those units, and create the navigational backbone that readers and publishing systems depend on.

The heading hierarchy is expressed through levels: a top-level heading (Heading 1) names a major section; each lower-level heading (Heading 2 through Heading N) names a subsection within its parent. This ranked sequence carries the same structural meaning regardless of the format it is expressed. The level communicates the section's position in the hierarchy; the text communicates its subject.
The following table lists the heading styles and their corresponding DITA output:

row.entry: .ditamap file with matching title; .dita concept, task, or reference topic with content.
.dita topic nested inside the Heading 1 sub-map. Type classified by content.
.dita topic nested inside the Heading 2 topic. Type classified by content.

conbody.p: Only a semantically marked heading — applied through the document's native heading mechanism — creates a genuine section boundary that a converter, search engine, or publishing system can detect and act on.

In a .docx file, the built-in Heading styles are paragraph styles — Heading 1 through Heading N — each carrying an outline level attribute. The outline level is a zero-indexed integer: Heading 1 carries outline level 0, Heading 2 carries outline level 1, and so on.

The converter reads the heading outline levels in sequence and uses them to construct the root DITA map tree. The heading 1 or outline level 0 is used to create sub ditamaps <mapref> nested in the root DITA map. The subsequent outline level 2 to N generates nested topic files <topicref>. And the content between one heading and the next becomes a single .dita topic file (concept, task, reference and so on).

The sub Ditamap and respective topics are organized in the sequential order to establish the parent-child map relationships between topics and create the navigational backbone in the published output such as PDF or Online document.
conbody.note: A gap in the heading sequence — for example, a Heading 3 appearing directly under a Heading 1 with no Heading 2 between them — causes the converter to promote the lower-level heading. A multi-level heading sequence with empty paragraphs (no context) will generate empty DITA topics or map to <topichead> - altering the intended hierarchy in the output. Never use bold Normal style to simulate a heading. Bold formatting is purely visual and carries no structural meaning that the converter can read. Always apply the correct Heading style.
